chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn Sulayman from a man from the people of al-Jazira, known as Abu Muhammad, who said:

A man asked Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) while I was listening, and he said to him: 'May I be your ransom, indeed Allah the Exalted says: "And if he is of hardship, then deferment until ease." Tell me about this deferment that Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book, is there a known limit for it? When this insolvent person becomes so, is it necessary for him to be deferred, and this man has taken the wealth of this person and spent it on his dependents, and he has no revenue whose arrival is awaited, nor a debt whose due date is awaited, nor absent wealth whose arrival is awaited?'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, he is deferred to the extent that his news reaches the Imam, so he pays what is upon him from the share of the creditors, if he spent it in obedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. And if he spent it in disobedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, then he has nothing from the Imam.'

I said: 'Then what is for this man who entrusted him, and he does not know whether he spent it in obedience to Allah the Mighty and Majestic or in His disobedience?' He said: 'He strives for him in his wealth and returns it to him, and he is humble (or: in a humble state).'

key_terms.ذُو عُسْرَةٍ: The insolvent person (one who lacks means to pay)

ai.seo_question: How does the Imam determine the deferment period for an insolvent debtor who spent borrowed money?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) clarifies that the Quranic deferment for the insolvent debtor (mu'sir) is not indefinite but contingent upon the Imam's authority to adjudicate the debtor's expenditure. He establishes a theological distinction: if the wealth was spent in obedience to God, the debtor remains liable to creditors; if spent in disobedience, the Imam assumes the debt, effectively forgiving the debtor. This ruling highlights the Imam's role as the ultimate arbiter in financial disputes, ensuring justice while considering the debtor's spiritual state.
